translation:
_Dehi darshan sab ko kare, sabad darshan nav hoy,
sabad darshan bin jivana, paar na pahonchya koy ||1||_ (Everyone can behold a person's outward form, but the vision of the Word does not come this way. Without the vision of the Word, life reaches no one to the far shore.)

That is to say: in the path of devotion there should be no worship of a person as an individual. The Guru's position is important indeed, but if we take to worshipping only him as God, it becomes like discarding gold to buy iron. Today we see, in many places in society, how deeply people have sunk into worship of individuals; many have even lost their own power of discernment. To such blindly faithful devotees Maharaj Jivanji gives this warning: do not defile devotion by taking a mere person to be God Himself, the Manifest One, or a direct incarnation of Parbrahm. And if anyone gets himself called the Manifest One or God, he ought to be shunned. For it is of such men that Kabirji speaks:

_Kabir gadi baitha mahant kahave, baitha pooja khay,
kol hokare otare, khod khod mar jaye ||26||_ (One who sits upon the seat and calls himself mahant sits there and consumes the worship offered to him — he is like a burrowing mole that digs and digs and dies in its own digging.)

_Kabir dikhya leeni shikh bhaya, kari muktiki thaan,
sadguru to khoja nahi, thook bharaya kaan ||27||_ (Kabir says: he took initiation and became a disciple, and set his resolve on liberation, but he never truly sought out the true Sadguru — so only spit filled his ear.)

That is: one should not be led astray by someone's outward pomp and show. Otherwise, falling into the wrong hands is like a merchant who buys fake goods and later regrets it — so too, one who sets out to cross this ocean of worldly existence ends up drowning in it instead, and becomes an object of ridicule in society. Many people, going to buy gold cheap, lose both their real gold and their money, and afterward find themselves in a state that can neither be spoken of nor endured. It becomes, further, like the thief's mother weeping with her face buried in the grain-bin. Rather than fall into such a state, one should seek out a true Sadguru and receive devotion from him. From a guru who merely blows a mantra into the ear, only his spit will reach that ear — the true Name of Ram is never obtained from such a false guru. Such gurus are born taking the incarnation of a "kol", a large burrowing rat. So, to show what difference there is between a true Sadguru and a so-called guru, Kabirji says:

_Kabir sabad sabad kaha karo, sabad ko haath na paanv,
ek sabad okhad kare, ek sabad kare ghaav ||2||_ (Kabir says: keep speaking of the Word — the Word itself has neither hand nor foot, yet one Word acts as medicine while another Word inflicts a wound.)

"Aushadhi" (herb-medicine) removes disease. The Manusmriti, Chapter 1, verse 46, says that plants bearing abundant flowers and fruit, which die once the fruit has ripened, are called "aushadhi". Fruit that ripens and falls of itself — barley, chickpea, wheat and other such grains — belong to this class. Ten grains of the field together are called "sarvaushadhi", the all-herb group: these ten grains are — 1) dhanya (grain/rice), 2) jav (barley), 3) til (sesame), 4) adad (black gram), 5) sauva, 6) cheno (a millet), 7) ghau (wheat), 8) masur (lentil), 9) vatana (peas). [As printed, only nine grains are listed though the text says "ten".]

By speaking words that sound pleasant, people show sympathy; by uttering harsh, bitter, cutting words, people run to strike in anger. In the same way, taking God's Name brings well-being, while uttering impure incantations brings downfall. The Panchatantra, in the Kakolukiyam, verse 111, says:

_Rohate sayakair viddham chhinnam rohati chasina,
vacho durruktam bibhatsam na prarohati vaakshatam ||9||_ (A limb pierced by arrows heals; a wound from a sword also heals. But a heart pierced by speech never heals. Therefore harsh words should never be spoken.)

_Vakya baan nahi chhodiye, tikshanta yoon tu joy,
katu vachan Kuru kul hanyo, Bhim krodh vash hoy ||28||_ (The arrow of speech should not be loosed — see how sharp its force is: because of one bitter word, Bhim, overcome with anger, destroyed the whole Kaurava clan.)

_Dukh na hata sansarmen, hata na shok viyog,
sukh hi men dukh la diya, boli bole log ||29||_ (There was no sorrow in the world, nor grief, nor separation — but people, by speaking such words, brought the pain of grief and the separation of loved ones into what had been happiness.)

How great a difference there is between one word and another! The Guru's word is a form of graciousness, while the hypocrite's word is like a wound, exceedingly painful. To show whose words cause such a wound, Govinddas states in the Sarvangalila:

_Je sant sabad mane nahi, eh ohalanghe aap,
dasha bhulo daaladriyun bohotu kahego baap ||3||_ (Whoever, out of ego, does not follow the Saint's teaching but transgresses it — that poor soul, having lost the true direction, will, from suffering so much distress, cry out again and again, "Oh father, oh father!")

One who transgresses the Saint's words becomes directionless and greatly sorrowful, for a man intoxicated with his own conceit heeds not even the saintly precepts — such as the scriptural words "speak truth, practice righteousness, speak agreeably" — and the like. Such a man becomes very unhappy. Moreover, one who does not conduct himself according to dharma behaves as though wounding others: he himself becomes unhappy, and the person he faces becomes unhappy too. Here it has been shown how one who transgresses the Saint's words behaves like one dealing a wound. Now Maharaj Jivanji shows how the Saint's words are, by contrast, like medicine.

_Daarki chuki baandari, shabadka chukya hans,
sabhaka chukya pandita, teenoka nirvansh ||30||_ (If a female monkey misses her branch, if the soul forgets the Guru's spoken teaching, and if a scholar slips in an assembly or examination — all three meet complete ruin.)

_Tavad askhalitam yavat sukham yati same pathi,
skhalite cha samutpanne vishame cha pade pade ||10||_ (A man can walk on level ground without stumbling only as long as he walks with ease; but once he loses his footing and strays from the path, he stumbles at every single step.)

_Char mukti mide bhai, jahan prem bhakti prakash,
jivan mugat jan Jivana, jahan sadguru shabad vishwas ||4||_ (Maharaj Jivanji says: when I received the light of loving devotion, I set aside all four kinds of liberation. When faith is placed in the Sadguru's teaching, then even while living a devotee's life one becomes free from every kind of worldly bondage.)

Maharaj Jivanji says:

_Gyaan kathe so baavra, mukti mage so moodh,
prem bhakti bin Jivana, jamki phaansi praudh ||31||_ (Those who keep speaking of attaining divine and self-knowledge are all frantic and out of their minds; and those who beg for liberation are foolish and lacking understanding — for even attaining such knowledge or liberation without loving devotion, they will certainly fall into the terrible noose of death.)

Kabirji says: one who, for the sake of liberation, takes refuge in divine knowledge or ritual religious duty, only wanders lost in the darkness of Maya.

_Kabir deepak pragata premka, jahan sadguru shabad prakash,
andhiyara sab jagatkun, jahan karma dharmaki aash ||32||_ (Baba Kabirji says: when the light of the Sadguru's teaching is received, the lamp of loving devotion is lit; but where people, without love and devotion, merely walk the path of ritual duty — japa, tapa, vows and the like — hoping thereby to attain God, such worldly people only stumble about in the darkness of delusion and attachment.) Maharaj Gnaniji says:

_Sant sangat je janiye, jake dradh vrat Hari naam,
char mukti mage nahi, or vaikunthko dhaam ||33||_ (Maharaj Gnaniji says: know that whoever has taken a firm resolve to recite the divine Name has kept true company with saints. Such devotees ask for none of the four kinds of liberation, nor even for the abode of Vaikuntha.)

Kabirji says:

_Kabir mugat na maagun bhagati na chhandun, Hari gun sunat sunaun,
Ram Krishna avatar manorath, janam janam gun gaun ||34||_ (Baba Kabirji says: I do not ask even for liberation, nor will I ever give up devotion to God — I shall hear and recount the glories of Hari. May Ram and Krishna go on taking incarnation, and birth after birth may I sing their glories and perform their devotion — such is my longing.)

Vyasji says:

_Vyas char mugat bilakhat phire, Shri Vrindavanki khor,
mohe baas kyun na Vrajmen diyo, main neerkhun jugal kishor ||35||_ (All four kinds of liberation wander about, restless and distressed, in the narrow lanes of Vrindavan, saying: "Why did God not grant us the privilege of dwelling in Vraj? Had He granted it, we too would have enjoyed the bliss of beholding Shri Krishna.")

_Salokya-sarshti-samipya-sarupyaikatvam aayutam,
diyamanam na grihnanti vina matsevanam janah ||11||_ (Bhagavat, Skandh, Adhyaya 29, Shlok 13 — Even when offered the five kinds of liberation — salokya, sarshti, samipya, sarupya and sayujya, oneness — desireless devotees do not accept them by forsaking My service.) (Salokya = dwelling in the same realm as God; sarshti = attaining opulence equal to God's; samipya = staying near God; sarupya = attaining a four-armed form like God's; sayujya, oneness = merging with God as the Ganga's water merges with the ocean. This is stated in order to establish faith in the Sadguru's word:)

_Parkho guruka shabadko jo guru kahe vichar,
bina shabad kachhu na mile, dekho nayan nihaar ||36||_ (Understand well the teaching that the Guru gives after deep thought — without this teaching nothing at all is attained; open your eyes and see for yourself.) Hence it is said:

_Apne apne dharmame, dradh raho sab kaal,
nij dharma paale rahe, saheje bhaya nihaal ||37||_ (Always remain firmly established in your own dharma; one who continues to observe his own dharma easily attains fulfillment — his boat crosses over.)

In the treatise on Maya and Brahm, Maharaj Jivanji does not accept the four kinds of liberation, namely: 1) salokya, 2) sarupya, 3) sanidhya, 4) sayujya. In this sakhi he states that none of these four kinds of liberation have any real meaning, because a person who has not learned how to truly live his life in this world, whose living has become sheer poison, with what face can he speak of attaining happiness after death? This is nothing but hypocrisy. One whose life lacks love, devotion, and light is, though living, as good as dead.

Even many highly religious people are unable to truly live their lives. That one ought to live according to dharma is a hundred percent true statement. But what true dharma is — that is extremely difficult to understand. Those who, under the influence of religion, become blindly faithful and turn timid or cowardly have never truly lived; there is nothing more to them than a soft, mushy sheep. Just as we speak of karma-yoga, jnana-yoga and bhakti-yoga, so too a "life-yoga" — a discipline of living — should be recognised. If a religion makes a person cowardly or spineless, then no matter how widespread that religion is, and however good it may appear, it is not worthy of acceptance. So now we explain the nature of that love, devotion and light, and of the Sadguru's Word. The essence of the Supreme Being may be reckoned subtler even than the atom and the sub-atomic particle — so fine, so subtle, has it been known within life.

_Pushp vaaspe patla, aisa prem prakash,
roop rekh nahi Jivana, jahan darshan pave das ||5||_

_Kabir paani seti patla, dhunva seti jheen,
pavan beg utaavla, so dost Kabire keen ||6||_

The Sadguru has shown the vision of Parbrahm in the form of the Word: that He is finer even than the fragrance of a flower's scent, subtle, without shape or outline — and yet the devotee-servants of God do behold the vision of this loving light of Parbrahm. Kabirji says: that Supreme Being is thinner than water, finer than smoke, and swifter than the wind — such a Parbrahm is Kabirji's friend; that Supreme Truth I have attained.

_Kabir sant santoshi sarvada, sabad bhed suvichaar,
ta par sadgurukee daya, sahaj seel su mat saar ||7||_

_Kabir Ram baith vichariya, sevak tu shabash,
muj sarikha tuj paas hai, pan tu so nahin muj paas ||8||_

The devotee marked by loving devotion, reflecting on the secret of the Sadguru's teaching, remains ever content, always pleased with whatever he has received. Through the grace of the ever-watchful Sadguru, he attains the natural state and the finest of the finest, a devotion-filled understanding. Seeing such a devotee, God, praising him, says:

Seeing such a devotee of firm character and steadfast faith in the Guru, this thought came to Ram: "O devotee, you deserve praise, for even one such as I remain present and manifest before a devotee like you — but I have no other devotee as steadfast as you; scarcely one such may exist; your like I find nowhere else."

Kabirji says:

_Sajan ham na bisariya, jo tum bahut milaaye,
muj jaisa tere bahut hai, tuj jaisa mere naahi ||38||_

Kabirji says: I went searching for another like God, all the way to the ocean, but the Imperishable Supreme Being was one alone; whereas Kabirs like me existed on the earth, and yet, in the very waters of the ocean too, I saw crores of Kabirs like myself. This astonished me — what kind of Kabir dwells in the ocean, and what kind on its shore, is not something one can grasp; nor what the essence of the Kabir dwelling in a body might be. But then I understood: wherever there is one who receives the Sadguru's teaching, there too are souls who attain God.

In this sakhi, regarding the wondrous nature of God, Kabirji says it cannot truly be understood in what manner God, in His qualified aspect, dwells within the soul, and in what manner He, in His unqualified aspect, also dwells within the soul. Kabirji reflects deeply and repeatedly upon God; one incident is worth considering.

Dadu-ji's guru, Rajab-ji, was a Brahmin. He was on his way to be married; the wedding procession was passing. Someone asked Kabir Sahib, "What is this that is going?" He said, "A tanner is going." Hearing this, Rajab-ji got down from his horse and said, "I am a Brahmin — why do you call me a tanner?" Kabir replied: "Whatever trade a man follows, he is named accordingly — for example, a carpenter goes to fetch wood, but you are going to fetch skin, so you are a tanner" (since, through marriage, he was about to obtain a person of bone and flesh). At this, understanding dawned on him; he touched Kabir Sahib's feet and took his teaching.

Dadu-ji then thought: "Everywhere such special praise is given to Kabirji — are other saints then not gifted?" With this thought he resolved to go where Kabir's name would not be heard. Thinking so, he set out by boat upon the sea; there, in the middle of the ocean, a fish uttered a sound.

_Sant pariksha lenkun, gaye samudra teer,
gyani machhi mukh suni, ratat Kabir Kabir ||39||_ (A saint like Dadu-ji went all the way to the ocean to test Kabirji; but by his own understanding it became clear, on reflection, that even the fish living in the water could be heard chanting "Kabir, Kabir" — that is, everywhere in the world, in every single soul, devotion to God and God's own reflection are present.)

Dadu-ji says:

_Kaun Kabir jalmen base, kaun samudra teer,
sapt dweep nav khandmen, kete hai Kabir ||40||_ (What kind of Kabir-essence dwells in the water, the unqualified, formless aspect of God; and what kind resides on the ocean's shore, the qualified, embodied aspect? On the whole earth, of seven continents and nine divisions, how many such Kabir-forms of God are there?) — so Dadu-ji began to ask. The fish says:

_Sohi Kabir jalmen base, sohi samudra teer,
sapt dweep navkhandmen, ek hi Ram Kabir ||41||_ (The very God-essence present as Kabir in the unqualified aspect is present too in the qualified aspect. Therefore, in the whole created earth of seven continents and nine divisions, the God-essence — Ram-Kabir — is one and the same essence; for God, there is no difference between the qualified and the unqualified.)

When God, praising a devotee like Kabir, said, "One like Me is with you, but no other one like you is with Me," Kabirji said:

_Kabir dhundhat dhundhat main phira, sant samudra teer,
avinashi to ek hai, muse kot Kabir ||9||_ (O Lord! Searching for one like You, I went all the way to the ocean's shore, but You alone are the one Imperishable God like You; while of ones like me, crores were found — devotees like me who worship You with single-minded devotion.)

Saint Dadu has also written a similarly humble sakhi:

_Tumkun hamse bahut hai, hamkun tumse naahi,
Dadukun jani pariharai, tun rahu naina hun maahi ||42||_ (Dadu-ji says: O Lord, before You there are many like me, but before us there is no other merciful one like You. So never abandon a lowly devotee like me — I wish to keep You within my very eyes.)

Yet Kabirji, contrariwise, also says the opposite — it is his nature to speak both crosswise and straight.

_Dware tere Ramji, milahu Kabira mohi,
tain to sabme mili raha, main na milungaa tohi ||43||_ (O God! At Your door, devotees like me will indeed be found; but You pervade everywhere, present within everyone — yet I shall not be able to find You in that "everywhere".)

Thus Kabirji at one time says there is no other God like You in the world, and again says You dwell everywhere in the world — speaking, as it were, in reverse with God. Kabirji, moreover, sets at nought even the gods and other such beings.

_Indralok achraj bhaya, Brahma bada vichar,
Kabira chala Ram pai, kautuk kahar apaar ||44||_ (When such a soul, leaving behind attachment to sense-objects, set out to meet Ram, wonder arose in Indralok — the pleasure-loving gods fell into astonishment; and Brahmaji, absorbed in worldly activity, seeing this soul free of worldly entanglement, fell into deep thought, considering it more fortunate than himself; and a profound wonder occurred everywhere.)

It is said in a doha:

_Mere to tum ek ho, tumhare or anek,
sarovar hansa bohot hai, hansa sarovar ek ||45||_

The lake is one and the swans many, but whichever swan goes to the lake and takes refuge there, the lake surely grants it shelter. The king is one and the queens many, but whichever queen, through body, mind and wealth, conducts herself so as to please the king and truly becomes his — that queen gradually brings the king under her sway, so that gradually the king becomes hers.

_Kabir kaha Kabir jalman base, kaha jalki teer,
kaha Kabir ghatman base, jyun shabad tyun Kabir ||10||_ (My understanding tells me: the Supreme Reality in the form of Kabir dwells in the water, and dwells also on the ocean's shore — that is, there is no difference between the qualified and unqualified, embodied and formless aspects of the divine. So the unqualified God-essence in the form of Ram, and the qualified, embodied form of God as Kabir, are not different; this Ram and Kabir are one and the same.)

_Kabir herat herat heriya, sudh na rahi heraye,
boond samani samudrame, so ku heri jaaye ||11||_

_Kabir herat herat heriya, sudh na rahi heraye,
samudra samani boondmen, so ku hera jaaye ||12||_ (Kabirji says: searching, searching for the divine essence, I searched until, in that search, all awareness itself was lost — for how can it be understood that an ordinary soul became absorbed into a Parbrahm as vast as the ocean? Moreover, how can it be understood that the Supreme Reality, as vast as the ocean, has become contained in a small body like a mere drop — and yet has indeed become contained in that creature?)

For the person who has become free of the sense of duality, and who has offered his all into the Sadguru's words, his natural, virtuous character is now what is essential — that is, the qualities of the "sthitaprajna", the one of steady wisdom, that Krishna described to Arjuna: one whose every desire has, at all times, come to an end; whose mind, fixed upon a single object, need think of nothing else; who is unmoved by happiness or sorrow — upon such a one the Sadguru's mercy and compassion rain down, unceasing.

God says: "Kabir, I must go to devotees like you." For devotees, God is very easily accessible; but for God, obtaining a true devotee is very difficult. That is exactly why Kabirji says it is a matter of great wonder that in the whole ocean, drops of water become absorbed — but here, the entire ocean has become absorbed within a single drop. That is: if the soul, with the support of Parbrahm's Name, relinquishes the body, it attains Parbrahm, becomes absorbed into Him. But here the reverse has happened: Parbrahm, who pervades all moving and unmoving creation, has become absorbed into the tiny, subtle soul. Kabirji asks: what is this? He himself answers:

_Kabir boond samani samudrama, te jaane sab koy,
samudra samana boondmen, te chinhe virla koy ||13||_

_Kabir herat herat he sakhi, main gai samudra teer,
jeti boond samudramen, te te das Kabir ||14||_

_Kabir balihari us doodhki, jame nikase ghiu,
sabad ek Kabirka, so chaar bedka jeev ||15||_

_Kabir dil mila dayal so, tab kachhu antar naahi,
pala gali pani bhaya, yon Harijan Hari maahi ||16||_

_Kabir santka mata ek hai, doojaku ant na paar,
ek sabadmen sab kachhu, santan koti hazaar ||17||_

_Kabir adhar jalechu adhar dhar, adhar aash vishwas,
adhar Kabira hi mile, adhar nirantar baas ||18||_

_Kabir kartam karta na hota, na hota hat aur pat,
tabtha Kabir Ramjan, jine dekhayo ghat ghat ||19||_

_Kabir paani pavan ambar nahi, na hota Omkar,
tabka das Kabir hai, so kaha jane sansar ||20||_

_Kabir sabad teta boliya, je gaya jahan chal,
sabko aap aapne mukhse, jahar kari majal ||21||_

_Kabir vachan hu the paiye, chor sahuku ghaat,
jesi bast bhajanmen, so nikase mukhki vaat ||22||_

Kabirji says: that the soul, like a drop, can become absorbed into the Supreme Being, like the ocean — everyone can understand that. But that the Supreme Being, like the ocean, can also become absorbed into the soul, like a drop — only some rare one, like a Sadguru, can explain that.

That one drop of water is absorbed into the ocean is easy to understand, but that the whole ocean should be absorbed into a single drop is difficult to understand. Yet, for the meditating person, in the matter between soul and Supreme Being, precisely this happens. In the meditating person absorbed in devotion, the inner sky of the heart, the innermost self, is like a single drop — within it he is able to see the Supreme Being, or the whole universe. In a heart that has become pure and illumined, the reflection of the entire universe can be seen. This subject of yoga, or the wholly absorbed devotee, is extremely profound, and so only rare, true devotees can understand it. The supreme devotee says:

_Bartan chhota vast ghana, kaho guru ka kije,
champ dharun to bartan phoote, bahar dharun to chhije ||46||_ (O Guruji! The vessel that is my heart is small, and the substance that is the Supreme Being is abundant — if I press and fill it in, the vessel will burst; if I keep it outside, it spills over. What remedy is there for this? Please show me.)

The Guru says:

_Sejalna sejan deena, sej surat lolai,
sejanvar to Kabirji, bartan kare samai ||47||_

The little bed of the heart, prepared for the Supreme Being to lie upon, is one on which God is made to lie with total absorption. The one who spreads such a bed of absorption is the supreme, most excellent Sadguru, Kabirji — a Guru so capable that he can make the Supreme Being become contained within this vessel that is the heart. The all-pervading, formless Lord — a capable devotee causes Him, in His qualified embodied aspect, to become contained within the Name. The Name of Ram is greater even than Ram himself.

Kabirji says: my attention, searching for God and for others like Kabir, went all the way to the ocean's shore, to the very end — and there it was found that in every single drop of the ocean's water there is only Kabir, Kabir. That is, drop by drop, throughout the whole world, each devotee has been given such power that God must remain subject to them. I am not Kabir alone; every single thing in the world, just like Kabir, holds God in its sway.

Kabirji says: just as the milk from which ghee is obtained is greatly praiseworthy, so too, of the words formed from the fifty-two-lettered alphabet, bad words bring us harm while good words bring us great benefit. Such is the wondrous virtue of this milk that is the alphabet — that the words which come to us as teaching, through the Guru, in the form of God's Name, bring about our well-being. Not only that, but the single word "Ram" that a Sadguru like Kabir has given is so important that, because of it, even the honest-merchant-thief, the four Vedas, receive the gift of life in this world. If the Vedas were to remove a word like "Ram", they would become lifeless. The Vedas have stolen the word "Ram", yet, since they still possess this stolen good, they are able to remain relevant in the world.

Maharaj Jivanji says that the Vedas have stolen the word "Ram":

_Ola jhola Jivana, je sadguru diya bataay,
karma dharmaman Raghupati, je vede dharya chhapaay ||48||_ (Gurudevko Ank 13 — The Sadguru, having resolved the tangled mystery hidden behind the veil, showed us the true essence. That true essence was the Name of Ram, which the Vedas had concealed within the practice of ritual duty — recitations, austerities, vows, pilgrimages, sacrifices and the like — but he opened it up and showed it to us. Thus the Vedas, deceiving through ritual religion, are the "honest-thief".)

Kabirji says: when our inner self becomes united and blended with the merciful God, then no difference remains between the unqualified Supreme Being and the qualified soul — just as water becomes ice, there is no real difference between Hari and Hari's devotee. When the ice of the ego melts, it merges into the water.

Kabirji, on the union of heart with the Merciful One, says in a Holi hymn:

_|| Hori ||
Jab dil milyo dayal so, tab kachhu antar naahi sakhiri || teka ||
Sahaj bhav upaje sahi ho, kahe na koi patiaay,
aham vyadhi sanso hare, aur aavaagavan nasaay ||1||
Surati sarovar gyan jal, naana var tarang,
aapa mitai to mile saain, tujhe mile tero rang ||2||
Ankur birvan phool phal, sab dekhe ek thaanv,
chit chetan kare chete ho, tab kaha le dhariye naav ||3||
Het deep sadguru milai, prem preeti prakash,
jwar virah na paaiya, jako kahe Kabir vilaas ||4||_

O friend! When our inner self becomes united and blended with the merciful God, then no difference remains between us and the formless Supreme Being. Natural love truly arises — were we to speak of it, no one would believe it. The disease of the fault of ego is cured, and the cycle of coming and going departs. In the lake of longing, many beautiful waves of the water of self-realization arise, and one attains the joy of one's own love. The tree of love, its sprout, its flowers and its fruit are all seen in one and the same place. When the awakened soul stirs into consciousness, whose Name should be taken? — then the Sadguru comes to meet us, carrying the lamp that casts the light of loving devotion. But if the pain of the fever of separation is not felt, Kabirji calls that mere pleasure, not true love.

The Saint's teaching is solely for the worship of the one Parbrahm, the Supreme Being; whereas all the other teachings of the Vedas, Puranas and scriptures never come to an end — they are endless. But the saints have taught that the sum total of crores and thousands of kinds of instruction is contained within the single word "Ram-Naam" alone.

"Adhar" — beyond the gunas, transcending them; "duliya" — path; and "ghar", dwelling — the state beyond the body: in Parbrahm, in that state beyond all the gunas, where there is no need even to place trust in any particular quality, Kabir the devotee ever dwells; the devotee remains in a state transcending the three gunas.

When there was neither any kind of Maya in the universe, nor Brahma nor other creators, nor the traffic of coming-and-going and dwelling in the womb, nor even the path of ritual karma — even then, God's saintly ones had existed from time immemorial. Such saints have shown the true nature of this Supreme Being as pervading every body, in vessel after vessel, throughout creation.

Kabirji says: when there was neither wind nor water, nor even Om itself — when in this creation only Parbrahm existed and nothing else — even then, the devotee Kabir was present with Parbrahm; the whole world knows this.

Whatever desires and cravings, whatever feelings arose within a being's inner self, that being's inclinations began to run after those very feelings. In this way each and every soul, through its own inward face, manifested its journey of dwelling in the womb in this world, according to its own feelings.

"Sahukar", the honest merchant, here means one who separates people from the Sadguru's family; and "thief" means one who leads people astray, deceiving them within this three-gunas'd creation — the one who devises the schemes of ritual observance, recitations, austerities, vows, sacrifices and the like, to lead people toward the heavenly realms. Such a person, harbouring deceit, does not speak the truth; he utters scripturally-worded speech only to entice and deceive. From this alone it becomes evident whether he is a thief or a genuine person. But it is the Sadguru who reveals who is true and who is false — for whatever substance a vessel holds, that same substance comes out through its opening.

The Vedas too have practised the trade of "honest-thief". By saying that performing a certain sacrifice yields a certain fruit, and other such enticing, sweet-sounding words, they entangle people in ritual observance. Even the Gita condemns the scholars who take interest in the Vedic path, and the doctrine of the Vedas itself (Bhagavad Gita, Chapter 2):

_Yamimam pushpitam vacham prapadyantyavipashchitah,
Vedavadaratah Partha nanyad astiti vadinah ||42||
Kamatmanah swargapara janmakarmaphalapradam,
kriyavishesha bahulam bhogaishwaryagatim prati ||43||_ (O Arjuna! Those absorbed in worldly desires, who consider heaven and heavenly pleasures the supreme, sole attainable good, become attached to the fruit-promising words of the Vedas and say there is nothing better than this. Such undiscerning people, in order to attain the enjoyment- and opulence-bearing states that yield the fruits of action across births, describe the many kinds of ritual actions set forth in the flowery, fruit-praising language of the Vedas — words that display abundant temptations of reward — and keep speaking such sweet, enticing words.)

Thus the Vedas too have practised the work of deceiving through sweet talk. But Sadguru Jivanji has exposed openly the theft and concealment that the Vedas have committed.

_Ola ola Jivana, jai sadguru diya bataay,
karma dharmaman Raghupati, je vede dharya chhapaay ||13||_ (Gurudevko Ang — what the Sadguru showed and revealed was the Lord Raghupati, whom the Vedas had kept hidden within the practice of ritual religion; that he brought to light.)

That deceit which confused us and cast us into wandering — the deceit by which the Vedas hid Raghupati within the rites of ritual duty — the Sadguru has revealed the Name of Ram that lay concealed within it.

The point is that a discerning person will immediately understand, from someone's manner of speech, whether that person intends to deceive. Sadguru Maharaj Jivanji has declared that no one should get entangled in the cleverness of the Vedas. It is through speech and conduct alone that a loyal person or a deceiver is recognised.

_Nari kahave piuki, rahai aur sang soi,
jaar purush hirde basai, khasam khushi kyon hoi ||49||_ (A woman calls herself her husband's wife, but if she keeps lying with another man and a paramour dwells in her heart, how can her husband remain pleased with her?)

One who worships his chosen deity with true faith, and one who secretly worships some other god, will each in time be recognised for what they are.

The Sadguru's words should be like milk, for from milk the finest thing, ghee, is obtained; likewise, if nothing is gained from the Guru's words, they are useless. So Kabirji says there is not much substance in the words of the Vedas — not all of the Vedas is acceptable. With each single word of Kabir's, as it were, the incomplete gurus, pandits and mullahs of the Vedic tradition are struck down. The devotee's heart and meditation are joined with Parbrahm; there is no gap between the devotee and God — just as ice melts and becomes water, there is no fundamental difference between ice and water, their inner composition being one and the same. Such is the relationship between Hari and Hari's devotee. Saints proceed solely on the basis of the Sadguru's words; there is no difference of opinion among them, however many thousands of saints there may be — whereas among scholars and pandits there is never unanimous agreement (the Narada Bhakti Sutra states that devotees of single-minded devotion are foremost, Sutra 67).

Kabirji says: when there was neither earth nor sky, I was present with Parbrahm, contained within Him — that is, at the time of dissolution the entire universe remains contained within Him, and creation is generated out of Him.

To those who hold faith in various scriptural doctrines, Kabirji says: when there was neither wind, water, nor sky, and not even Om — after that period of dissolution, creation came into being. Who then was there to witness it, or from where did creation arise? The various things we talk about today have no real meaning. Therefore, instead of delighting in false illusion, one should seek out the true Sadguru and take shelter in Hari.

Kabirji says: as is the mind, so is the word that is spoken — from the mouth of one with impure intent comes the denial of Parbrahm, while from the mouth of a saint no foul word ever comes. In this way every person is recognised by his manner of speech; it is through utterance alone that a thief and an honest merchant are recognised. As is a person's occupation and his deed, so is the word that comes from his mouth. Even if the word "Ram" comes from the mouth of a thief or a base person, it goes to waste, and in time he is recognised for what he is.

_Kabir bhaari kahun to bohu darun, halka kahun to jooth,
main kaha janun Ramkun, nayana kabahun na deeth ||23||_

_Kabir deetha hai to kis kahun, kaha kon patiyaaye,
Hari jaisa hai taisa hi hai, tun harkhi harkhi gun gaaye ||24||_

_Kabir aisa adbhoot jan katho, adbhoot rakhi lo koye,
Ved kateb na lakha, so kaha kon patiyaaye ||25||_

_Kabir hase na bole unmani, chanchal mahela maar,
kahe Kabir bheetar bheda, sadguru ke hathiyaar ||26||_

_Kabir Ram beth vichariya, sakhi kaho Kabir,
bhavsagarmen doobtan, ko ek paave teer ||27||_

Kabirji says: how can I say what Shri Hari is like? If I call Him heavy, mighty and weighty, I am greatly afraid; if I call Him light, simple and innocent, I would be speaking falsely, for these two eyes of mine have never seen Him. To behold Parbrahm one needs divine sight — without that, Hari cannot be seen.

And even if I had seen Him, to whom could I tell it, for who would believe me? Today is not an age for the truthful — it is the hypocrite and the false pretender who is worshipped. So, rather than asking what Hari is like, let Him be whatever He is — devotees should set aside all such disputes and simply sing His praises out of love for Shri Hari alone.

No one will be able to say that He is such-and-such a wondrous being — let everyone simply hold that He is wondrous, for such a Being has not even been described in the Vedas or in the Kateb (the other scriptures) — that is, they too do not know Him, so who then can explain Him?
